Higher level and Standard Level internal assessment
The range and suitability of the work submitted
As we close a cycle to move on to the new curriculum, many observations remain pertinent even when
criteria change.
The 2025 curriculum emphasises the criteria associated with using critical thinking (Conclusion and
Evaluation), and Communication has been integrated into the other criteria. Mathematical requirements
are also more clearly defined, and all skills and applications distributed throughout the programme will
be expected in the IA.
In the current curriculum, discrepancies often resulted from a shallow consideration of requirements that
allow reaching upper bands and the need for more use of the model of best fit. Some large cohorts showed
inconsistent marking, reinforcing the need to make an internal moderation.
The number of database investigations decreased, with a slightly higher number in Spanish. A common
problem was the limited number of databases used or comparable data collected. The criterion for
selecting sources was generally those giving similar values rather than discussing dispersions and reasons
for those.
Very few home-based investigations were submitted, and they were mostly of low quality due to the low
precision of instruments used.
Investigations have shown increasing progress in the complexity and quality of some of the investigations
undertaken by the most capable candidates since the beginning of the curriculum cycle. Some samples
were ambitious but needed an equally rigorous exploration and analysis.
In some cases, the research questions were very sophisticated, but with solid evidence that the student

A few investigations showed perfect data even when the method described evidenced very weak

validate the marks.
Unfortunately, many investigations were based on classic procedures, and interesting or novel ideas were

Overall, the diversity in topics of investigation is an area of concern.
There was a slight increment over previous sessions in comparative studies on brands, teas, coffees, kinds
of milk, types of fruits, and vegetables. As finding a relationship among those samples as independent
variables is way beyond the purpose of an IA investigation, this results in the repetition of a technique on
different samples and, while still of some educational value, provides limited material for the analysis of
the relationship between variables. Some schools submitted investigations based on subjective scales or
purely qualitative, which are not suitable to assess with the criteria.
Some predominantly biology or physics-based investigations were scored highly by the teacher, but
where the actual chemistry was expected at this level, and the selection of variables was limited.
Fewer investigations using simulators were submitted in English, though still several among those in
Spanish. These often
controlled or changed.
Few investigations were based on computational chemistry, and a common problem was reporting
insufficient data or using tools meant for visualisation only.
All tools must be available on an open-access site so moderators can access them.
Only a handful were too simple to meet the 10-hour lab work requirement.
Even fewer investigations only included a cover sheet or the procedure, with no evidence of covering the
minimum requirements for this mandatory component.
A few investigations included the extraction of some potentially toxic substances, the use of pesticides
related to vitamin C content or very hazardous solvents, e.g., chloroform for the extraction of the analyte,
or even swabbing of school toilets to acquire microbes to study the antimicrobial activity of alcohols or

in a school lab environment.
Most reports were supported with teacher criteria marks and comments; however, many reports did not
include annotations showing the primary marking, comments on how teachers arrived at their decisions,
and the aspect of the report considered for awarding higher or lower marks. Very often, the awarded marks
resulted from using only some descriptors, and the use of the model of best fit was rare. This made it more
difficult to validate marks.

Personal Engagement
More teachers looked beyond the introductory paragraph that tries to justify a personal reason for
choosing the topic, and their marks were validated more often than in previous sessions.
Two was awarded more often in this session because students could relate their investigation to the real
world and reflect their interest and initiative throughout the investigation. The initiative was frequently

Ex2- The requirements for the background are that it must be focused and contain relevant information
that is clearly linked to the research question.
Background information was often generic and not focused on the problem under study, providing
information on the nutritional advantages of a nutrient or textbook descriptions of pH and redox titrations.
Weaker candidates presented long paragraphs on the physical properties and methods for synthesizing a
reagent, a historical background, or disconnected paragraphs from different sources without using critical
thinking.
The background usually did not address their chosen independent variable (IV) in the context of their
investigation and often lacked balanced equations associated with the experiment. Many reports failed to
address the methodology used.


In brand analysis, candidates tend to focus more on the biology or physiology related to the topic, with
little development of the chemistry involved.
Many reports continue inserting structures whose characteristics are not used in the investigation and,
thus, superfluous.
In the case of databases, an explanation of the choice of data sources is required.
When using simulations and databases, candidates need to describe and explain the data selection and
collection process and include annotated screenshots of the simulations and the database controls. The
students also need to discuss the reliability of the sources for the databases and the simulations.
There are still a number of reports with null and alternative hypotheses included. Null and alternative
hypotheses, ANOVA, and t-tests (and similar) are allowed but not encouraged if enough data (above 10)
are planned to be collected. An incorrect approach affects this criterion, A1, and usually, A2 and Ev1.
This section is usually referenced, but teachers are encouraged to check the sources. Reliable resources
are expected by default, and the investigation should only include those that are directly related to the
investigation and have been actually used.

While one sample is needed for each calculation, all data must be reported. Raw data from data logging

Students must include experimental and qualitative data when they have entered theoretical ones in the

minimum of two concordant values is required for each point.

Statistical analysis, rarely relevant at this level, could have been better done. There should be some
evidence of calculations (could be a screenshot of software/picture of the calculator) for statistical tests,
not just the general formula. For statistical tests of this kind, establishing the probability level (p-value) is
a part of their outcome. For correlation coefficients, it is an additional step that needs to be considered. If
used, ANOVA should also be accompanied by a post-hoc test (e.g., Tukey test) so that the student can
determine the significance of the difference between the treatments. For significance tests that generate
a p-value, 0.05 or 5% level is taken as the critical value below which the results can be said to have
significance. Above this level, the results could be due to random chance.
Some students informed their calculations were done in Excel and just showed results, making it

students who had applied a method and collected data that

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students

Further comments
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching programme.
  There will not be sufficient time left for revising or repeating a method.

• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.

The strengths and weaknesses of the students in the treatment of individual
questions
Question 1
Responses were split between A, B, and C, demonstrating that candidates did not have a clear
understanding of molecular-level processes involved with changes of state.
Question 2
The correct response, D, was answered correctly by just over 50% of the candidates. As all responses
were alkenes, the question tested the relationship between empirical and molecular formulas.
Question 3
56% of responses were correct, identifying this question as a limiting reactant using gas volumes.

Half of the candidates correctly identified the smallest downward arrow as the spectrum's red line. One-
quarter of responses chose D the transition ending on level one.

Most candidates correctly identified the relationships between electronic configuration and period table
position.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
Candidates should be encouraged to use appropriate terminology, for instance, when to use hydroxy or
hydroxyl group instead of hydroxide, and distinguishing clearly between elements, atoms and nuclei.
Chemical terminologies should be taught carefully with enough practice and examples of application of
keywords for each topic.
Candidates should be encouraged to show working clearly for calculation-based questions, with the
correct number of significant figures and units. They should start with the formula or equation rather than
a jumbled array of numbers, and make it as easy as possible for an examiner to follow their working to
award ECF marks where applicable.
Where self-study is practiced for option topics, time should be taken by teachers to stress key points and
keywords required. Concepts that require understanding and application should be explicitly taught.

Standard level paper three
General comments
Over 5300 candidates sat this paper and, like last year, candidates found the paper very challenging with
the mean mark again being ~10/35 (29%). This was however quite skewed by the small number of higher
scoring candidates, so over 60% scored <10; the mode was 5 (14%). As commented last year, this is
noticeably different to May 2019, and the preceding years, when the mean was ~13 (37%), with a much
smaller proportion of candidates achieving a mark of 5 or under. It seems that students found Section A
particularly difficult, with the mean mark being <4/15 (25%). This is significantly lower than the equivalent
Section A mark in May 2019, when the mean was >6 (43%). Could this be an indication that current
candidates are carrying out fewer laboratory based investigations?
Sadly only 69 teachers took the time to complete the feedback form. About half of these felt the paper

difficult. It was however considered to be of appropriate level by ~80%, whilst the remainder thought it
was too difficult. The clarity of wording, presentation and readability of the paper were considered to be
of a good or very good standard by about 60% of teachers, whilst about 40% regarded them as acceptable
and a couple rated them poor. Teachers considered the papers good (~70%) or acceptable (~30%) for
suitability and inclusivity. Negative comments were mainly related to a lack of clarity about exactly what
was required for some of the questions in Section A, and these will be addressed in those questions.

The range and suitability of the work submitted
As we close a cycle to move on to the new curriculum, many observations remain pertinent even when
criteria change.
The 2025 curriculum emphasises the criteria associated with using critical thinking (Conclusion and
Evaluation), and Communication has been integrated into the other criteria. Mathematical requirements
are also more clearly defined, and all skills and applications distributed throughout the programme will
be expected in the IA.
In the current curriculum, discrepancies often resulted from a shallow consideration of requirements that
allow reaching upper bands and the need for more use of the model of best fit. Some large cohorts showed
inconsistent marking, reinforcing the need to make an internal moderation.
The number of database investigations decreased, with a slightly higher number in Spanish. A common
problem was the limited number of databases used or comparable data collected. The criterion for
selecting sources was generally those giving similar values rather than discussing dispersions and reasons
for those.
Very few home-based investigations were submitted, and they were mostly of low quality due to the low
precision of instruments used.
Investigations have shown increasing progress in the complexity and quality of some of the investigations
undertaken by the most capable candidates since the beginning of the curriculum cycle. Some samples
were ambitious but needed an equally rigorous exploration and analysis.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
• Read the questions carefully before attempting to answer, do not rush to put pen to paper. Doing so
  led to mistakes, for example in 3b(i) not reading sodium oxide and using a sulfur oxide in the chemical
  equation; in 3 (c) ii, not reading that what had to be suggested was the composition of a buffer
                                                               with units" had to be provided.
• Go beyond learning a definition by heart. For example, when asked to define a bond, the first idea is
  that it the result of an electrostatic attraction, so this cannot be omitted ever if the concept is
  understood.
• Learn organic reaction mechanisms, understanding the importance of drawing curly arrows accurately
  as they represent the specific movement of electrons.
• When writing equations for electron transfer at electrodes in electrolytical cells, understand that the
  direction of the arrow indicates the product, thus "Na → Na+ + e- " is not showing that Na is produced at
  the electrode but the contrary. This was a very common mistake.
• Topics/Concepts that should be considered carefully: knowledge/understanding of resonance,
  bonding, use of units, significant figures vs decimal places (even if not examined).
• Stress the need to check units carefully.
Communication:
• Try to answer within the space provided or use extra sheets of paper, clearly indicating this in the
  provided box.
• Draw diagrams with the correct type of pens provided.
• Try to ensure handwriting is legible.

Higher level/standard level internal assessment
The range and suitability of the work submitted
This session was the beginning of a new cycle, and it was gratifying to see that most schools followed
IB procedures meticulously, and many supplied a completed criteria marks sheet with criterion-level
comments for every student. However, a few schools omitted the accompanying marking notes or
rationales, making it difficult to gauge how they had applied the assessment criteria. Some large
cohorts showed inconsistent marking, reinforcing the need to make an internal moderation. Still,
some teachers only included comments that sing praise: while this support may be helpful during
the course, they are misleading in the final copy and fail to hide obvious lacks and mistakes.
A sizeable percentage of investigations showed that the teacher did not fully understand the new
criteria; for example, a whole page on personal engagement was not uncommon. Partials to some
strands, for example, Ev, were sometimes downgraded because strengths or extensions weren’t
suggested. These are no longer requirements in the current curriculum and, therefore, should not
impact marks.
Quite a few schools used ‘in-house’ documents to support their marks. While some endorsed the
Teacher Support Material (TSM) Guidelines, others didn’t, resulting in, at times, severe discrepancies.
It wasn’t helpful when the teachers just copied-pasted the descriptors without clearly showing their
best-fit approach to the final decision. In some cases, using a long list of numbers 1,2…, and sticky
notes in separate documents or at the beginning of the reports made it very difficult to follow the
teacher’s comments and rationale. At times, the sticky notes covered data or results.
Few reports mentioned that the work was done in groups and even fewer gave details about the
chosen variables by all group members and specified the uniqueness of their investigations
compared to their group members.
Candidates seemed more comfortable with the 3000-word limit and often resulted in higher quality
material. Unfortunately, in some schools, this led to graphs, tables, and images of unreasonably large
sizes. Including many images that didn’t add value, or too many tables. This approach often resulted
in work that complied with the word limit but covered 30-35 pages. Exceedingly large tables and
graphs may be as challenging to moderate as extremely tiny ones.
Most topics were suitable, but the implementation sometimes resulted in a low level of challenge,
resulting in very basic investigations that did not allow candidates to demonstrate data processing
skills. In other cases, the topics were too direct, i.e. their outcomes were well established, so it was

C1:
Most students presented a described, instead of justified, conclusion relevant to the research
question (and addressed their hypothesis if one had been presented) but not entirely consistent

Teacher’s marking was often found generous when the conclusion was based on limited processed
data.
A recurring weakness was that, after producing processed datasets and tidy graphs, candidates
seldom examined them closely with specific data references or discussed anomalies, which pulled
down their scores. Few students identified outliers and then decided to eliminate them judiciously,
clearly providing their rationale. Very often, only one of several outliers was identified, and students
frequently confused outliers with anomalies.
The emphasis here was often on explaining the results and their impact on the issues mentioned in
the background information, i.e., health and industrial processes. Extrapolation of ‘in vitro’
investigations into complex physiological processes was common ignoring the significant
differences between both contexts.

students forced the processing and conclusions to support their hypothesis.

and students are expected to understand its relevance. Some analysis is expected if the value is high,
but all error bars overlap.
A few still find it challenging to accept no correlation and often contradict themselves.
Candidates struggled to interpret data dispersion and distinguish it from instrument uncertainty.
The indistinct use of precise and accurate continues to be an issue.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
  individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
  the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
  Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
  descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
  numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
  teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
  pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
  program when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental program that introduces and practices the skills the students need for the
  IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
  difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
  of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
  opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
  known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
  Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
  standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
  depth and ownership.

  methodology and vague terms, e.g.’ extent’ and ‘efficient’.
• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
  for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
  variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
  having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
  theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
  reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
  each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
  and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
  specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical
  theory relates to their investigation, how their independent variable could affect the dependent
  variable in their context and the theory and methodology required to study this.
• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable
  sources.
• Students should ask themselves if the proposed method allows them to answer their research
  questions before collecting data. It’s equally valid to change the procedure or the research
  question, however, in the last case should also check if the presented background continues to
  be relevant.
• Students should carefully consider efficient sampling. For example, measurements on just one
  tablet can’t be considered representative.
• Students should be aware that incorrect storage of their samples may invalidate their data and
  conclusion.
• Check that the collected data is adequate to answer the research question, and if not, modify the
  latter in terms of the technique implemented and the data gathered.
• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.
• Students should check that their databases have sufficient data to perform a reasonable analysis
  before fully engaging in their investigations.
• Foster the practice of having the students prepare at least three separate samples for each
  independent variable and measure each instead of measuring the same solution three times when

  meaningful connection to chemical principles.

  argumentation beyond mere experimental results, addressing the observed weakness of
  insufficient theoretical backing.

  should provide specific evidence from their investigation and assess each limitation’s impact on
  the results’ reliability and validity. A more in-depth analysis could be fostered using checklists and

Standard level paper two
General comments
Paper 2 covered a broad and representative range of syllabus content, and overall the paper was
considered accessible and well-balanced by teachers. While a significant number of candidates were
able to engage effectively with recall-based questions, performance varied markedly on those
requiring application, interpretation of data, and multi-step calculations. Also, the widespread lack
of precision in definitions, diagram labelling, and chemical terminology hindered candidate success.

The areas of the programme and examination which appeared difficult for
the students
Several conceptual and procedural weaknesses were repeatedly observed: - Definitions lacked
scientific accuracy and completeness; terms such as "element", "compound", and "ionic bonding"
were poorly defined, and distinctions between similar concepts (e.g., ion movement vs. electron
movement) were often blurred. - Writing and balancing redox and half-equations, especially in
electrolysis contexts, posed major challenges. Candidates struggled with correct electron transfer,
states, and charges. - Organic chemistry remains a major hurdle, particularly in identifying functional
groups, applying nomenclature, and recognizing isomerism (including functional group isomerism).
- Multi-step quantitative problems revealed poor calculation structuring, missing or incorrect units,
and a lack of significant figure awareness. Common errors included using Celsius instead of Kelvin
in gas law problems and misapplication of molar ratios. - Students often misunderstood questions
or failed to respond to all components, indicating a lack of familiarity with command terms and
examination expectations.

The areas of the programme and examination in which students appeared
well prepared
There were notable areas of strength: - The bonding triangle, identification of bonding types from
diagrams such as the Van Arkel triangle, and explanations involving catalysts and energy profile
diagrams were generally well understood. - Candidates often performed well in recall-based
questions, including stoichiometry, drawing energy profiles, determining molecular geometry, and
stating equilibrium constant expressions. - A number of students demonstrated competent use of
the ideal gas law, though issues with units and conversions were still common. - Physical chemistry
topics such as rate, equilibrium, and basic enthalpy concepts were comparatively better handled.

The strengths and weaknesses of the students in the treatment of individual
questions
Question 1: In part (a), many candidates were unable to provide accurate definitions of “element”
and “compound.” Responses often lacked clarity and specificity—for example, stating that a
compound is “composed of one atom” rather than “atoms of different elements chemically bonded

components of equilibrium expressions. In part (b)(ii), candidates struggled to comment
meaningfully on the relationship between Kc and equilibrium position. Many assumed that a shift in
equilibrium must correspond to a change in Kc, reflecting a misunderstanding of Le Chatelier’s
Principle. Part (b)(iii) also revealed confusion. While colour changes were often described (e.g.

could produce a fully correct equation, with the majority failing to balance electron transfer. This
may reflect inadequate practice with half-equations in unfamiliar contexts. In part (b)(i), while the
general distinction between ionic and covalent bonding was made, many relied on vague statements
such as “ionic means transfer and covalent means sharing,” without reference to electrostatic
attraction or specific particles involved. In part (b)(ii), drawing the nitrate ion structure proved very
challenging. In part (b)(iii), while some correctly identified molecular geometry, others gave
meaningless shape descriptions (e.g., “square” or “line”) even for single-atom ions, indicating

Question 5: Part (a), involving combustion analysis, was one of the weakest questions across the

poorly understood—few mentioned the correct alcohol product (RCH₂OH). In part (c)(i), while most
students could identify the correct compound, many forgot to indicate carbon positions with
numbers (e.g., 1,2-dibromoethane). In part (c)(ii), the idea of electron density in the C=C bond was
often missed, with students instead referencing vague ideas like “weak bonds.” Part (c)(iii) was
generally well answered. In part (c)(iv), most candidates linked boiling point trends to molar mass
and London dispersion forces, though some confused intermolecular with intramolecular forces.
Part (c)(v), a calculation question, yielded mixed success. Many gained partial credit, but a full, correct
solution was rare due to transcription errors, or flawed logic.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
Emphasise precision in scientific language and definitions. Teachers should ensure students
understand key terms and distinctions through regular low-stakes quizzes and peer marking using
IB command terms. - Focus more on exam technique: how to approach multi-part questions,
highlight command terms, interpret question scaffolding, and organize multi-step working logically.
- Improve literacy in chemical equations: practice ionic and redox equations frequently, emphasizing
states and correct electron flow. Use model kits and visual resources to enhance understanding of
3D bonding and Lewis structures. - Organic chemistry instruction should include hands-on tasks for
naming, drawing isomers, and identifying functional groups. - Use past mark schemes rigorously in
internal assessment and mock exams to condition students to the level of detail and precision
expected. - Encourage students to read the entire question carefully before attempting an answer.
Incorporate comprehension-focused activities within chemistry lessons to develop this skill.

Higher level/standard level internal assessment
The range and suitability of the work submitted
This session was the beginning of a new cycle, and it was gratifying to see that most schools followed
IB procedures meticulously, and many supplied a completed criteria marks sheet with criterion-level
comments for every student. However, a few schools omitted the accompanying marking notes or
rationales, making it difficult to gauge how they had applied the assessment criteria. Some large
cohorts showed inconsistent marking, reinforcing the need to make an internal moderation. Still,
some teachers only included comments that sing praise: while this support may be helpful during
the course, they are misleading in the final copy and fail to hide obvious lacks and mistakes.
A sizeable percentage of investigations showed that the teacher did not fully understand the new
criteria; for example, a whole page on personal engagement was not uncommon. Partials to some
strands, for example, Ev, were sometimes downgraded because strengths or extensions weren’t
suggested. These are no longer requirements in the current curriculum and, therefore, should not
impact marks.
Quite a few schools used ‘in-house’ documents to support their marks. While some endorsed the
Teacher Support Material (TSM) Guidelines, others didn’t, resulting in, at times, severe discrepancies.
It wasn’t helpful when the teachers just copied-pasted the descriptors without clearly showing their
best-fit approach to the final decision. In some cases, using a long list of numbers 1,2…, and sticky
notes in separate documents or at the beginning of the reports made it very difficult to follow the
teacher’s comments and rationale. At times, the sticky notes covered data or results.
Few reports mentioned that the work was done in groups and even fewer gave details about the
chosen variables by all group members and specified the uniqueness of their investigations
compared to their group members.
Students seemed more comfortable with the 3000-word limit and often resulted in higher quality
material. Unfortunately, in some schools, this led to graphs, tables, and images of unreasonably large
sizes. Including many images that didn’t add value, or too many tables. This approach often resulted
in work that complied with the word limit but covered 30-35 pages. Exceedingly large tables and
graphs may be as challenging to moderate as extremely tiny ones.
Most topics were suitable, but the implementation sometimes resulted in a low level of challenge,
resulting in very basic investigations that did not allow students to demonstrate data processing
skills. In other cases, the topics were too direct, i.e. their outcomes were well established, so it was
more of a verification. Some schools, and unfortunately not a very small number of them, chose to
compare brands or the locations where the material was collected rather than engaging in more
chemical concepts. This situation was more frequently observed with schools new to the system.
Investigations based on simulators or secondary data were infrequent. Students rarely followed the
TSM guidelines and hardly ever scored highly. Students sometimes used sophisticated software with

Conclusion
C1:
Most students presented a described, instead of justified, conclusion relevant to the research
question (and addressed their hypothesis if one had been presented) but not entirely consistent
with the data.
Teacher’s marking was often found generous when the conclusion was based on limited processed
data.
A recurring weakness was that, after producing processed datasets and tidy graphs, students seldom
examined them closely with specific data references or discussed anomalies, which pulled down their
scores. Few students identified outliers and then decided to eliminate them judiciously, clearly
providing their rationale. Very often, only one of several outliers was identified, and students
frequently confused outliers with anomalies.
The emphasis here was often on explaining the results and their impact on the issues mentioned in
the background information, i.e., health and industrial processes. Extrapolation of ‘in vitro’
investigations into complex physiological processes was common ignoring the significant
differences between both contexts.
Sometimes, the link between results and research questions was done qualitatively. At other times,
students forced the processing and conclusions to support their hypothesis.
Students often justified the correlation found using the values of R 2 but rarely went beyond stating
it was a ‘strong correlation’ without explaining the suggested value. It wasn’t rare to see students
considering values as low as 0.3 to be moderately strong. No ‘ideal’ value exists for this coefficient
and students are expected to understand its relevance. Some analysis is expected if the value is high,
but all error bars overlap.
A few still find it challenging to accept no correlation and often contradict themselves.
Students struggled to interpret data dispersion and distinguish it from instrument uncertainty. The
indistinct use of precise and accurate continues to be an issue.
Assumptions were rarely addressed.
Many students find error classification, a required T3 skill, challenging and discussing errors’ impact
was usually shallow. While weaknesses and limitations are assessed in Ev, this criterion requires
considering random and systematic errors and the latter’s direction here. However, many students
presented this analysis in the Ev section, and credit was given.
C2:
It was often poorly attempted, and it wasn’t rare to see a repetition of the information in RD1, which
doesn’t allow the work to reach the middle band.

The weakest section in most reports was rarely in the top band because students often struggled to
identify and discuss the significance of limitations or propose realistic improvements.
It is still often a table with a list of limitations/weaknesses and improvements without discussion. At
best, the evaluation is descriptive instead of explained as the criterion requires.
Teachers are often rewarded with extremely generous marks and comments extended lists of
limitations or weaknesses and the corresponding improvements that should have been addressed
during the design. These may not reach the middle band in both strands.
Hypothetical and generic weaknesses were often suggested, and improvements in conditions that
were not previously reported.
Many students included “strengths” and “further investigations” in the report. These aren’t a
requirement, and it’s the teacher’s choice to include them, but they shouldn’t impact marks. In some
cases, though, the strengths discussed the impact of errors on results, and credit was given in C1.

Few students correctly classified errors as systematic or random, and even fewer explained their
direction (there was frequent confusion between both).
The students evidenced a vague idea of the differences between limitations and weaknesses.
Ev2:
Improvements were often generic, procedural and unrealistic, or lacking alignment with the
previously identified weaknesses. At times, they were not related to these.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
  individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
  the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
  Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
  descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
  numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
  teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
  pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
  programme when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental programme that introduces and practices the skills the students need for
  the IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
  difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
  of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
  opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
  known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
  Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
  standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
  depth and ownership.
• Students should be encouraged to remain within the 10-hour work period for the assessment.
  More complex work with multiple independent variables rarely benefits students in terms of their

• Discourage overambitious research questions that cannot be answered with the proposed
  methodology and vague terms, e.g.’ extent’ and ‘efficient’.
• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
  for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
  variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
  having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
  theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
  reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
  each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
  and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
  specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical
  theory relates to their investigation, how their independent variable could affect the dependent
  variable in their context and the theory and methodology required to study this.
• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable
  sources.
• Students should ask themselves if the proposed method allows them to answer their research
  questions before collecting data. It’s equally valid to change the procedure or the research
  question, however, in the last case should also check if the presented background continues to
  be relevant.
• Students should carefully consider efficient sampling. For example, measurements on just one
  tablet can’t be considered representative.
• Students should be aware that incorrect storage of their samples may invalidate their data and
  conclusion.
• Check that the collected data is adequate to answer the research question, and if not, modify the
  latter in terms of the technique implemented and the data gathered.
• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.
• Students should check that their databases have sufficient data to perform a reasonable analysis
  before fully engaging in their investigations.
• Foster the practice of having the students prepare at least three separate samples for each
  independent variable and measure each instead of measuring the same solution three times when
  manipulating the independent variables.
• Students should master the correct procedure of making standard solutions and dilutions using
  volumetric glassware.

• Discourage the use of pictograms that add minimum value.
• Encourage procedures to use lower quantities of chemicals to preserve the environment and

• If practical work is possible, encourage students to process and reflect on data while collecting it
  so they can immediately adapt or extend their procedural phase if the data are proving insufficient
  or erroneous. Also, processing data while it is being collected is always good practice.
• More emphasis is needed on the quality of data, and its dispersion can be seen as an opportunity
  to understand its impact and explore ways to deal with it. It is important not to just calculate it
  but then ignore it.
• Please verify that your students have collected the data they report.
• Provide targeted practice on graph analysis, trend identification, and using uncertainty and
  statistical tools. Teach students to critically evaluate their data rather than simply presenting raw
  results.
• The tools described in T3- Processing uncertainties and Graphing should be introduced early in
  the course and integrated into as many labs as possible.
• Dedicate time to teaching proper data presentation, particularly for tables.
• Discourage your students from implementing statistical analysis they don’t understand or lack the
  time to collect sufficient data.
• Double-check all calculations to identify any errors that might impact the reliability of the
  conclusions.
• When performing sample calculations, students should be encouraged to clearly state which
  experiment/trial they are based on.
• Students should try alternate best-fit lines before deciding on the final line that fits the data
  plotted.
• Discourage your students from eliminating outliers simply because their results or trendlines don’t
  match their original expectations.
• Teachers should emphasize that conclusions are not just results summaries but must include a
  meaningful connection to chemical principles.
• Instruct students on how to effectively integrate secondary evidence or relevant chemical theory
  to support and contextualize their conclusions. This will elevate their understanding and
  argumentation beyond mere experimental results, addressing the observed weakness of
  insufficient theoretical backing.
• Providing examples that model strong theoretical reasoning could help bridge this gap.
• Teach students that effective evaluations must go beyond listing weaknesses or limitations—they
  should provide specific evidence from their investigation and assess each limitation’s impact on
  the results’ reliability and validity. A more in-depth analysis could be fostered using checklists and
  encouraging phrases such as “this may have led to…” or “this could have significantly affected…”
  to show clear analytical reasoning. Teachers should gradually work with students to build these
  skills by analyzing sample investigations, discussing the strengths and weaknesses of hypothetical
  setups, and practicing the language of critique.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
• It is important to cover all parts of the syllabus equally well.
• Provide plenty of opportunities to tackle novel questions to ensure that your students can apply
  the concepts in new situations rather than memorize set procedures or answers.
• Include higher order thinking questions during the course.
• Use different approaches to ask questions about a concept so that the students do not memorize
  a specific method/answer but rather apply their understanding to each question.
• It is good practice to eliminate the distractors by working out what mistake each one represents
A possible approach to multiple choice exam
• Read the questions very carefully to make sure you aren’t missing valuable information.
• If you find the more mathematical questions challenging, leave them for the moment and return
  them after you have completed the questions with which you feel more comfortable.
• Allocate time for this section to ensure you have enough time for both sections.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
• Work on the importance of taking all the necessary time to read a question carefully and then
  answer specifically what is requested.
• Students need to understand the various command terms fully, and teachers should take time to
  review them (across all three objectives) with students throughout the two years of the
  programme to ensure they understand how to answer questions.
• Students should always look at the associated mark allocations in the questions. Together with
  the command terms, the marks provide guidance on the depth expected by examiners for each
  answer.
• Students are not required to answer questions in complete sentences. They may focus their
  responses on bullet points.
• Laboratory work must lie at the heart of the IB chemistry programme.
• Ideally, students should be exposed to comprehensive experimental experience in a laboratory
  with suitable facilities. Where this is not the case, other resources, such as simulated experiments,
  should be sourced.
• Time management should allocate enough time during the course to experimental skills, so
  students not only perform the required experiments but also have time to analyze experimental
  techniques in full depth and detail.
• Students should practice providing the correct names for different correlations.
• Drawing best-fit lines/curves with a focus on equal spacing of points.
• Students should use a ruler and an adequate pencil to draw lines on graphs.
• Students should be alert to the number of arguments/statements required by the question and
  avoid providing more to avoid penalizations resulting from the List Principle.
• Ensure that students recognize that a dependent variable is a measured variable. Values that are
  calculated are derived.
• Practice with the Tools of Chemistry to ensure familiarity with the techniques and processes
  mentioned in that part of the syllabus.
• Students should practice how to explain processes using the correct terminology.
• Ensure students are familiar with various types of contexts for titration, including redox titrations.
• Practice interpreting all kinds of graphs more extensively.
• Review equipment names and lab procedures frequently throughout the course.
• Practice explaining specific sources of error that are consistent with the directionality of the error.
• Teachers should make the students aware that converse arguments are accepted. For students
  answering in a second language, this may facilitate their argument-making score a mark.
• Students must be presented early on the course with simple investigations to identify possible
  sources of error and their impact on results and suggest realistic improvements. More complex
  investigations should then gradually follow this.
• Students should correctly identify the section of a question they are answering when using extra
  pages. For example, 1d wasn’t enough as there were five sections for 1d.

Section B

General comments
The introduction of Paper 1B brings a significant change to the external assessment model. It
primarily assesses the “Skills in the study of chemistry”. Compared to the 2016 curriculum’s
prescribed practical’s, students are now required to apply their practical knowledge more flexibly
and across a variety of different, unfamiliar contexts. Doing so often necessitates wordier questions
as the context of the question needs to be more extensively laid out.
Several teachers felt that the paper aligned well with the syllabus and placed greater emphasis on
practical skills compared to the legacy curriculum’s Paper 3 Section A. The feedback received on this
paper was very helpful and covered a variety of aspects including timing, question wording,
feedback on specific questions, use of command terms and overall impressions. Over 100 teachers
provided feedback on SL Paper 1B in this time zone. Thank you.
Over 90 % of teachers rated the difficulty level as appropriate, and just under 10 % felt it was too
difficult. Around 35 % of respondents found the paper to be a little or much more difficult than last
year. The mean mark achieved on this paper was 8.52 out of 25 possible marks.
In terms of inclusivity and suitability of the paper, around 80% of teachers considered it to be “good”
or “very good”, with the remaining responses rating it as acceptable. The comments described positive
reactions to the readability of the paper, with most questions perceived as clear and not excessively wordy.
The readability, presentation, and clarity of the paper were described as “good” or “very good” by
just over 80 % of teachers. A handful (2 %) indicated concerns in these areas. In the comments
concerns were raised relating to the presentation of the combined paper sections 1A and 1B as
students need to manage their time well as well as the various papers and resources on their desks.

General comments
This paper was of appropriate level by 90% of the 158 schools that responded to the G2 report,
among whom almost 60% considered it to be of similar difficulty to M24 and 25% found it a little
more or much more difficult. Other issues referred to qualities of the paper such as inclusivity,
suitability, readability, presentation and clarity were good or very good by 80% of schools. Being the
first session with the new syllabus that has introduced a significantly different approach, it was
interesting to find that teachers found that the exam reflected the more interwoven concepts of the
course through the themes of structure and reactivity for example. Many teachers considered it to
be a nice balance between familiar and unfamiliar contexts. While many teachers felt that there were
many calculations, which some students might have struggled with, they also felt that there were no
surprises—everything was within the core of the Chemistry syllabus.
One of the aspects to be noted is that the percentage of questions attempted was higher than in
previous sessions and even very weak students were able to provide reasonable answers to the few
questions they were able to answer. The questions that were answered incorrectly or left unanswered
were often common to very good students so it could be expected that they were either
misunderstood or too challenging. It is also possible that while they were topics that they were
familiar with, the combination of different aspects of chemistry of a compound or element which is
the basis of the new curricular approach is still not fully embraced by students and teachers alike.
A recurring comment from teachers referred to the fact that the language used in the paper was
concise and free of unnecessary complexity. Key instructions and questions were presented clearly,
aiding understanding for students who additional language learners are.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
• Firstly, some very practical points to avoid losing easy marks:
• Ions must be written as Xn+/- and oxidation states as X+/- n
• Rate always includes the mention of time.
• Check units: this is the most common mistake in calculations involving entropy, enthalpy and ∆G.
• Be aware of connectivity of atoms when drawing organic structures, such as in question 1di
  (acetonitrile).
• Unit conversions/decimal places: train students to read questions carefully in terms of command
  terms, units, and precision
• Pay attention to the change in requirements for answering the same type of questions. For
  example, "complementary colour of light absorbed" is no longer a point to get the mark.
• Pay attention to the requirements for significant figures.
• Encourage students to show all the calculations. Rounding must be done at the end.
• Practice in sketching and labelling graphs.
• Teach students to indicate the question clearly in the extra paper. It is quite common for an
  examiner to have to be following incorrectly numbered answers in extra pages.
• Keep answers concise: there seemed to be a significant increase in the number of students using
  the answer booklet to complete questions, however the style of the questions has not changed

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
• Teachers are strongly advised to refer to past examination papers and the corresponding mark
  schemes to assist students with examination preparation.
• Students should read questions carefully to avoid missing parts of the question. This ensures that
  they answer appropriately, precisely, and use correct terminology.
• Too often, students are not giving reasons for their answers, even though it is explicitly asked for
  in the question.
• For example, Q2a(iii): Explain why, in terms of nuclear charge and the shielding of the valence
  electrons, the first ionization energy of thallium is lower than that of lead, but a significant number
  of students are still missing out on the nuclear charge and shielding in their answers. The students
  are still writing “there are more collisions between molecules” without referring to time when
  explaining the increase in reaction rate.
• Teachers should encourage students to note the number of marks allocated to a question and
  correlate this to their response to ensure it is sufficiently detailed. This will enable students to

Higher level/standard level internal assessment
The range and suitability of the work submitted
This session was the beginning of a new cycle, and it was gratifying to see that most schools followed
IB procedures meticulously, and many supplied a completed criteria marks sheet with criterion-level
comments for every student. However, a few schools omitted the accompanying marking notes or
rationales, making it difficult to gauge how they had applied the assessment criteria. Some large
cohorts showed inconsistent marking, reinforcing the need to make an internal moderation. Still,
some teachers only included comments that sing praise: while this support may be helpful during
the course, they are misleading in the final copy and fail to hide obvious lacks and mistakes.
A sizeable percentage of investigations showed that the teacher did not fully understand the new
criteria; for example, a whole page on personal engagement was not uncommon. Partials to some
strands, for example, Ev, were sometimes downgraded because strengths or extensions weren’t
suggested. These are no longer requirements in the current curriculum and, therefore, should not
impact marks.
Quite a few schools used ‘in-house’ documents to support their marks. While some endorsed the
Teacher Support Material (TSM) Guidelines, others didn’t, resulting in, at times, severe discrepancies.
It wasn’t helpful when the teachers just copied-pasted the descriptors without clearly showing their
best-fit approach to the final decision. In some cases, using a long list of numbers 1,2…, and sticky
notes in separate documents or at the beginning of the reports made it very difficult to follow the
teacher’s comments and rationale. At times, the sticky notes covered data or results.
Few reports mentioned that the work was done in groups and even fewer gave details about the
chosen variables by all group members and specified the uniqueness of their investigations
compared to their group members.
Students seemed more comfortable with the 3000-word limit and often resulted in higher quality
material. Unfortunately, in some schools, this led to graphs, tables, and images of unreasonably large
sizes. Including many images that didn’t add value, or too many tables. This approach often resulted
in work that complied with the word limit but covered 30-35 pages. Exceedingly large tables and
graphs may be as challenging to moderate as extremely tiny ones.
Most topics were suitable, but the implementation sometimes resulted in a low level of challenge,
resulting in very basic investigations that did not allow students to demonstrate data processing
skills. In other cases, the topics were too direct, i.e. their outcomes were well established, so it was
more of a verification. Some schools, and unfortunately not a very small number of them, chose to
compare brands or the locations where the material was collected rather than engaging in more
chemical concepts. This situation was more frequently observed with schools new to the system.
Investigations based on simulators or secondary data were infrequent. Students rarely followed the
TSM guidelines and hardly ever scored highly. Students sometimes used sophisticated software with

Very rarely were dispersed values acknowledged, which is a common problem when working in
these conditions, and it was not the student’s fault. In this situation, the student could have worked
with concordant data but continued to use all values in DA3.
Still, students are attempting statistical tests with insufficient data, and unfortunately, some teachers
seem to expect students to do this.
Sometimes, students include many tables spreading across several pages, making it difficult to read
and understand. Some students presented data tables and processing in the appendix even when
the TSM clarifies, “All information relevant to the investigation must be presented within the report.

Students often included the general standard deviation formula when opting to use it instead of an
example with actual values.
Most students are consistent in decimal places within plus or minus one. However, when the decimal
place is inconsistent with the uncertainty, you wonder if the student understands what it tells them.
This lack of understanding was observed in several investigations, which reported one decimal place
more -and at times two- than the uncertainty and based their graphical analysis and conclusions on
differences in this decimal place.
This poor grasp was also patent with students who could reasonably propagate errors but worked
with data within the uncertain range.
In some schools, uncertainties weren’t reported in the raw data table or weren’t reported at all when
working with standard deviation.
Units missing in calculations or tables weren’t rare, and values in graphs often differed in precision
from those in tables and reported inconsistent decimal places. If this results from an unavoidable
lack of the software used, the student should briefly clarify.
Other common flaws were standard deviation with an excessive number of decimal places, unitless
when it shouldn’t be, and titles that weren’t specific or altogether missing.
Graphs and tables should be readable. Since they aren’t considered in the word count, there’s no
justification for tiny graphs or tables or for spreading the latter.
DA2:
 A wide range of approaches to uncertainties.
While neither a list, nor uncertainties in it are required, this approach works well for many schools.
However, students should check the values reported in the list and be consistent with those in the
raw data.

Stronger students also used the uncertainty bars to calculate the error in the gradient of the best-

DA3:
Most students were able to process their data to answer their research questions. Occasionally, there

Sometimes, students showed limited skills in graphical analysis, with questionable lines of best fit,

Conclusion
C1:
Most students presented a described, instead of justified, conclusion relevant to the research
question (and addressed their hypothesis if one had been presented) but not entirely consistent
with the data.
Teacher’s marking was often found generous when the conclusion was based on limited processed
data.
A recurring weakness was that, after producing processed datasets and tidy graphs, students seldom
examined them closely with specific data references or discussed anomalies, which pulled down their
scores. Few students identified outliers and then decided to eliminate them judiciously, clearly
providing their rationale. Very often, only one of several outliers was identified, and students
frequently confused outliers with anomalies.
The emphasis here was often on explaining the results and their impact on the issues mentioned in
the background information, i.e., health and industrial processes. Extrapolation of ‘in vitro’
investigations into complex physiological processes was common ignoring the significant
differences between both contexts.
Sometimes, the link between results and research questions was done qualitatively. At other times,
students forced the processing and conclusions to support their hypothesis.
Students often justified the correlation found using the values of R 2 but rarely went beyond stating
it was a ‘strong correlation’ without explaining the suggested value. It wasn’t rare to see students
considering values as low as 0.3 to be moderately strong. No ‘ideal’ value exists for this coefficient
and students are expected to understand its relevance. Some analysis is expected if the value is high,
but all error bars overlap.
A few still find it challenging to accept no correlation and often contradict themselves.
Students struggled to interpret data dispersion and distinguish it from instrument uncertainty. The
indistinct use of precise and accurate continues to be an issue.
Assumptions were rarely addressed.
Many students find error classification, a required T3 skill, challenging and discussing errors’ impact
was usually shallow. While weaknesses and limitations are assessed in Ev, this criterion requires
considering random and systematic errors and the latter’s direction here. However, many students
presented this analysis in the Ev section, and credit was given.
C2:
It was often poorly attempted, and it wasn’t rare to see a repetition of the information in RD1, which
doesn’t allow the work to reach the middle band.

should be like the conditions used in RD2.

teachers should not penalize additional information except if a student contradicts themselves.
Citations are not assessed using any criterion, and reference to the Teacher Support Material is
needed for issues of academic malpractice. It wasn’t rare to find bibliographies that had been ‘beefed
up’ with articles that, when checked, were unrelated to the focus of the investigation.
The use of unreliable sources or student sites should be discouraged.

Evaluation
The weakest section in most reports was rarely in the top band because students often struggled to
identify and discuss the significance of limitations or propose realistic improvements.
It is still often a table with a list of limitations/weaknesses and improvements without discussion. At
best, the evaluation is descriptive instead of explained as the criterion requires.
Teachers are often rewarded with extremely generous marks and comments extended lists of
limitations or weaknesses and the corresponding improvements that should have been addressed
during the design. These may not reach the middle band in both strands.
Hypothetical and generic weaknesses were often suggested, and improvements in conditions that
were not previously reported.
Many students included “strengths” and “further investigations” in the report. These aren’t a
requirement, and it’s the teacher’s choice to include them, but they shouldn’t impact marks. In some
cases, though, the strengths discussed the impact of errors on results, and credit was given in C1.
Ev1:
Few students correctly classified errors as systematic or random, and even fewer explained their
direction (there was frequent confusion between both).
The students evidenced a vague idea of the differences between limitations and weaknesses.
Ev2:
Improvements were often generic, procedural and unrealistic, or lacking alignment with the
previously identified weaknesses. At times, they were not related to these.
In some cases, they were vague, such as using a colourimeter or spectrophotometer, without a solid
explanation of why it would be better. Some very weak students suggested techniques that seemed
beyond their skills and in many cases, techniques not available at the school level were suggested.

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
Whenever possible, teachers should:
• Provide comments, partials, and an overall mark for each marking criterion. Holistic results of
  individual criteria often disagree with the use of partials and the model of best fit.
• Refer to the Teacher Support Material (TSM) for detailed guidelines.
• When the material is borderline in two criteria, choosing the upper band in one and the lower in
  the other is sometimes wise.
• Using grade descriptors can help determine if the overall mark has been too strict or generous.
• It’s very helpful if the work is annotated with the strands for each criterion, as shown in the TSM.
  Schools should rigorously adopt the “best-fit” model and avoid awarding high bands when any
  descriptor is unmet.
• Ensure that the work is anonymous. The candidate’s name, the school’s name, and the session
  numbers must all be removed before scanning and uploading, both from the candidate and the
  teacher’s mark sheet.
• Be careful when uploading the material. The work uploaded is the final one. Check that all the
  pages are scanned, and that symbols, equations and data are clear.
• Images, graphs and tables should be of a reasonable size.
• Do not schedule the action stage of the individual investigation for the end of the teaching
  programme when there will not be sufficient time left to revise or repeat a method.
• Plan an experimental programme that introduces and practices the skills the students need for
  the IA.
• Introduce the command terms in the assessment criteria to students so they understand the
  difference between state, describe, explain and justify.
• Show students some of the exemplary material and get them to use the assessment criteria.
• Get students to visualize/plan how to use the time provided for the practical part of the IA.
• Use the assessment criteria when providing feedback on other practical work.
• Teachers should approve only those investigations that allow students to satisfy the expectations
  of the set criterion clearly.
• Both teachers and students should carefully evaluate the choice of topics to see if it allows enough
  opportunity to carry out an in-depth investigation within the available time and resources.
• Topics beyond the curriculum can be encouraged with due support.
• Ensure that students are not repeating an experiment already carried out in the course.
• Ensure the investigation doesn’t stray from chemistry.
• In the absence of the Personal Engagement criterion, students are increasingly selecting safe, well-
  known topics. While this may ease the planning process, it limits critical thinking and originality.
  Teachers should encourage students to formulate research questions that, even if based on
  standard methodologies, reflect a personal angle or a specific variation that adds intellectual
  depth and ownership.
• Students should be encouraged to remain within the 10-hour work period for the assessment.
  More complex work with multiple independent variables rarely benefits students in terms of their

• Discourage overambitious research questions that cannot be answered with the proposed

• Including more than one research question and independent variable is rarely advisable except
  for databased investigations.
• Check that suggested ranges are consistent with the presented context.
• Guide students in selecting independent variables that are genuinely manipulable and dependent
  variables that can be measured with appropriate accuracy and precision.
• Independent variables should be quantified, and relationship study is highly recommended.
• Given the generally good performance in the Research Design criterion, students benefit from
  having a clear structure. Teachers are encouraged to emphasize key components such as
  theoretical background, safety, and procedural clarity. However, care should be taken not to
  reduce the task to a template-driven exercise — students should be guided to understand why
  each section is necessary, not just how to complete it.
• Provide structured support in planning without over-scaffolding.
• The background must be specific to the research question and the context of the investigation
  and not journalistic in nature. It should include all relevant chemical equations.
• Students should be discouraged from writing copious background information that does not
  specifically address their study’s context. Instead, they should focus on how current chemical
  theory relates to their investigation, how their independent variable could affect the dependent
  variable in their context and the theory and methodology required to study this.
• Avoid relying on a method proposed in any given source and check its validity with other reliable
  sources.
• Students should ask themselves if the proposed method allows them to answer their research
  questions before collecting data. It’s equally valid to change the procedure or the research
  question, however, in the last case should also check if the presented background continues to
  be relevant.
• Students should carefully consider efficient sampling. For example, measurements on just one
  tablet can’t be considered representative.
• Students should be aware that incorrect storage of their samples may invalidate their data and
  conclusion.
• Check that the collected data is adequate to answer the research question, and if not, modify the
  latter in terms of the technique implemented and the data gathered.
• Check the methodology for any missing key variable that would invalidate the conclusions drawn.
• Students should check that their databases have sufficient data to perform a reasonable analysis
  before fully engaging in their investigations.
• Foster the practice of having the students prepare at least three separate samples for each
  independent variable and measure each instead of measuring the same solution three times when
  manipulating the independent variables.
• Students should master the correct procedure of making standard solutions and dilutions using
  volumetric glassware.

• If practical work is possible, encourage students to process and reflect on data while collecting it

  or erroneous. Also, processing data while it is being collected is always good practice.
• More emphasis is needed on the quality of data, and its dispersion can be seen as an opportunity
  to understand its impact and explore ways to deal with it. It is important not to just calculate it
  but then ignore it.
• Please verify that your students have collected the data they report.
• Provide targeted practice on graph analysis, trend identification, and using uncertainty and
  statistical tools. Teach students to critically evaluate their data rather than simply presenting raw
  results.
• The tools described in T3- Processing uncertainties and Graphing should be introduced early in
  the course and integrated into as many labs as possible.
• Dedicate time to teaching proper data presentation, particularly for tables.
• Discourage your students from implementing statistical analysis they don’t understand or lack the
  time to collect sufficient data.
• Double-check all calculations to identify any errors that might impact the reliability of the
  conclusions.
• When performing sample calculations, students should be encouraged to clearly state which
  experiment/trial they are based on.
• Students should try alternate best-fit lines before deciding on the final line that fits the data
  plotted.
• Discourage your students from eliminating outliers simply because their results or trendlines don’t
  match their original expectations.
• Teachers should emphasize that conclusions are not just results summaries but must include a
  meaningful connection to chemical principles.
• Instruct students on how to effectively integrate secondary evidence or relevant chemical theory
  to support and contextualize their conclusions. This will elevate their understanding and
  argumentation beyond mere experimental results, addressing the observed weakness of
  insufficient theoretical backing.
• Providing examples that model strong theoretical reasoning could help bridge this gap.
• Teach students that effective evaluations must go beyond listing weaknesses or limitations—they
  should provide specific evidence from their investigation and assess each limitation’s impact on
  the results’ reliability and validity. A more in-depth analysis could be fostered using checklists and
  encouraging phrases such as “this may have led to…” or “this could have significantly affected…”
  to show clear analytical reasoning. Teachers should gradually work with students to build these
  skills by analyzing sample investigations, discussing the strengths and weaknesses of hypothetical
  setups, and practicing the language of critique.

General comments
Whilst most of the 36 teachers who completed the feedback form indicated that the paper was of
similar difficulty to the previous paper (56%) almost all the others (38%) rated it as easier. The

Recommendations and guidance for the teaching of future students
It is difficult to generalise about multiple choice errors, but many seem to arise from students
misreading the question, indicating the need to pay more attention to what is being asked.
The low marks on the last half dozen questions might indicate that students were running out of
time. Students should therefore regularly practice taking multiple choice tests in order to develop
their technique, particularly with regard to leaving questions they are having difficulty with until the
end, in order that they know how much time is available to spend on them. They do however need
to clearly mark such questions so that they always enter an answer to every question, even if it’s only
a guess!

Section B

General comments
This was the first ever sitting of a Paper 1b and the impression was that the nature of the paper
came as something of a shock to many students. There were a number of questions when the
answers given by a large number of students gave the impression they had not even managed to
comprehend the context in which the question was being asked. The lack of awareness of practical
situations, and how experiments are designed was worrying, perhaps indicating that many students
are not sufficiently familiar with many aspects of routine laboratory work. As a result the mean mark
of the just under 6000 students was just over 15/35; just under 43%.
Most of the 46 teachers who completed the feedback form felt it was of appropriate difficulty (80%)
whilst all the others (20%) considered it too difficult. This was the first ever Paper 1b, however
